hook.line: Tomás has the flu and everything aches. In Spanish the sore part does the work: your head hurts you, the same way *gustar* works.
hook.es: Me duele la cabeza y tengo fiebre.
hook.en: My head hurts and I've got a fever.

examples.en: Does it hurt a lot? (to a friend)

examples.es: A don Hernando le duele la rodilla.

rule:
*Doler* works like *gustar*: the body part does the hurting, so the verb follows the body part.

One thing: *me duele la cabeza*.
More than one: *me duelen los pies*.

Who's hurting goes in front: *me*, *te*, *le*, *nos*, *les*.

It's *la cabeza*, never *mi cabeza*: *me* already says whose.

Or use the noun: *tengo dolor de cabeza*, I've got a headache.
smallPrint: As with *gustar*, the body part is the subject of the verb.

yourTurn.why: *Me* says whose head, so it's *la cabeza*.

yourTurn.prompt: Ask a friend: Does it hurt a lot?
yourTurn.why: *Te* for a friend, and *duele* for the one thing that hurts.

yourTurn.answer: A don Hernando le duele la rodilla.
accept: Le duele la rodilla a don Hernando.
yourTurn.why: *Le* points at him, and *a don Hernando* says who.

yourTurn.prompt: Make it more than one: Me duele la pierna. (say: My legs hurt.)
Say it with the noun instead: Me duele el estómago.
yourTurn.why: *Dolor* is something you have: *tengo dolor de*.

pitfalls.why: Almost. *Me* already says it's yours, so the body part takes *la*.
The verb follows the body part: two feet, *duelen*.
*Dolor* is a thing you have, so *tengo dolor*.

personal: Does anything hurt today? Say what, with *me duele* or *me duelen*, or say *no me duele nada*.
